questions.q: The page prints what percentage of FTD (Pick's disease) as sporadic?
questions.exp: FTD (Pick's disease): 70% sporadic, young onset dementia (50-60 years), rapidly progressive dementia; note contrasts Alzheimer's -> 90-95% sporadic (cerebral atrophy MRI pair). (Book p577)

questions.q: FTD pathology involves the MAPT gene on which chromosome, with which m/c protein?
questions.exp: Pathology involves MAPT gene chromosome 17; proteins involved: TDP-43 (m/c), tau (hyperphosphorylated: loss of function of tau molecule) -> Pick's bodies, FUS; b/l prefrontal cortex atrophy. (Book p577)

questions.q: Loss of social embarrassment, apathy, impaired planning and judgement with relatively preserved memory - which FTD type is the m/c one?
questions.exp: Clinical features: m/c type behavioural variant; loss of social embarrassment; social and emotional systems dysfunction (apathy, overeating - temporal); impaired planning and judgement; memory relatively preserved; hyperorality - temporal lobe involvement. (Book p577)

questions.q: The side notes pair hyperphosphorylated tau with which diseases, and split the PFC into which three parts?
opts: CJD and Binswanger; ego, id, memory
PSP and MSA; attention, memory, motor
Alzheimer's and Pick's; Id, superego, ego
questions.exp: Notes: tauopathy -> hypophosphorylated tau / hyperphosphorylated tau (Alzheimer's, Pick's); PFC -> Id, superego, ego. Diffuse Lewy Body Dementia: 2nd m/c cause of dementia; part of Parkinson-plus/atypical Parkinson's syndrome. (Book p577)

questions.q: Which pairing lists only the 'alpha synuclein'-opathies in the Parkinson-plus components tree?
opts: Multiple system atrophy and diffuse Lewy body dementia
Progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration
questions.exp: Components of Parkinson plus syndrome: 'Tau'opathies - progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration; 'alpha synuclein'-opathies - multiple system atrophy, diffuse Lewy Body dementia. (Book p577)

questions.q: Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions whose content is:
questions.exp: Lewy bodies: intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions; content alpha-synuclein. Note: Parkinson's = alpha synucleinopathy; Alzheimer's = 'Tau'pathy (degenerated cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of meynert); anticholinergics are the Rx of drug-induced parkinsonism. (Book p578)

questions.q: Characteristic changes of 'alpha synuclein'-opathies precede disease onset by how long?
questions.exp: Characteristic changes 5-10 years before onset of disease: 1. REM sleep disorders; 2. autonomic nervous system symptoms - postural hypotension, erectile > ejaculatory dysfunction, urinary abnormalities. (Book p578)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the autonomic symptom NOT listed for 'alpha synuclein'-opathies:
questions.exp: Listed ANS symptoms: postural hypotension, erectile > ejaculatory dysfunction and urinary abnormalities. (Book p578)

questions.q: Cognitive impairment within 1 year of motor manifestations, visual hallucinations before motor symptoms, b/l axial rigidity with rocket sign, tremor uncommon, antipsychotics worsening, L-dopa unresponsive - which diagnosis?
questions.exp: DLB v/s PD table: DLB - cognitive impairment precedes/within 1 year (predominant rapidly progressive dementia), visual hallucinations and fluctuating alertness precede motor symptoms, tremors uncommon, b/l axial rigidity (rocket sign +), gait abnormalities common, antipsychotics worsen (d/t D2 receptor inhibition), L-dopa no improvement, treatment none available; PD - after 4-5 years of motor manifestations, tremor common, asymmetrical rigidity, gait uncommon, L-dopa improves, Rx L-dopa and deep brain stimulation. (Book p578)

questions.q: The rocket sign is defined in the note as:
opts: Falling backwards immediately after trying to get up from a chair
Forward lean on the pull test
questions.exp: Note: rocket sign - falling backwards immediately after trying to get up from a chair. (Book p578)

questions.q: Severe memory impairment, early dysphasia, apraxia/agnosia/acalculia present, visuo-spatial defects more severe, indifferent personality - which column of the comparison table?
opts: Subcortical dementia (examples DLB, PSP, NPH, Binswanger)
questions.exp: Cortical column: examples Alzheimer's, FTD; affected hippocampus, medial temporal lobe; memory severe; apraxia (superior parietal lobe lesion) / agnosia (association areas) / acalculia (angular gyrus) (+); early dysphasia; visuo-spatial more severe; personality indifferent; mood depressed (subcortical > cortical); coordination normal; cognitive and motor speed normal; abnormal movements rare; extrapyramidal symptoms -. (Book p579)

questions.q: The subcortical dementia column's affected regions are:
opts: Subcortical grey matter (basal ganglia, thalamus) and white matter (corticospinal, corticobulbar fibres)
questions.exp: Subcortical column: examples DLB dementia, PSP, NPH, Binswanger's disease; regions subcortical grey matter (basal ganglia, thalamus) plus subcortical white matter (corticospinal, corticobulbar fibres); memory less severe; language normal; personality apathetic; coordination impaired; speed slow; abnormal movements common; extrapyramidal symptoms +. (Book p579)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the row value NOT from the subcortical dementia column:
questions.exp: Subcortical column values: language normal (cortical: early dysphasia), personality apathetic, speed slow, abnormal movements common. (Book p579)

questions.q: Prion is defined on the page as:
opts: An infectious protein with no nucleic acid
A misfolded peptide carrying nucleic acid
questions.exp: Prion: infectious protein with no nucleic acid; genetic/sporadic. Pathology: beta-pleated PrPsc protein -> spongiform degeneration of cortex -> neuronal loss. (Book p579)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the prion disease NOT in the types list:
questions.exp: Types of prion diseases: 1. CJD, 2. familial fatal insomnia, 3. kuru, 4. Gerstmann Straussler Scheinker disease. Common features: young onset dementia, rapidly progressive dementia, no immune response. (Whipple's appears only in the p573 rapidly-progressive list.) (Book p580)

questions.q: CJD: spongiform cortical changes with cortical ribboning, basal ganglia hyperintensities, dementia with myoclonus, long incubation and no immune response - which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: CJD investigations: EEG - low voltage background, high voltage sharp waves; CSF normal; brain biopsy to confirm diagnosis; Rx flupirtine maleate (centrally acting non-opioid analgesic). (Book p580)

questions.q: The dementia-protein table pairs DLB with which protein?
questions.exp: Dementia-protein table: Alzheimer's A-beta; FTD tau; DLB alpha synuclein; CJD PrPsc. Vascular dementia: types large vessel disease (post-CVA dementia) and small vessel disease. (Book p580)

questions.q: Large-vessel vascular dementia: the m/c site of infarct per the page is:
questions.exp: Large vessel disease: m/c site of infarct b/l PCA lesion; criteria: 1. dementia; a. cerebrovascular disease - multi-infarct state with 'strategic territory' infarct (infarct in these areas leads to dementia). (Book p580)

questions.q: The 'relationship between the two disorders' requires dementia onset when after a stroke?
questions.exp: 3. Relationship between the two disorders: onset of dementia within 3 months of stroke; stepwise decline in cognitive function (stepwise graph). (Book p581)

questions.q: Binswanger disease pathology involves penetrating vessels of what size range?
questions.exp: Small vessel disease - Binswanger disease: most important risk factor HTN; lacunar infarct; pathology lipohyalinotic infarct involving penetrating vessels (size 30-300 um); MRI finding white matter hyperintensities in elderly (gradual cognitive-decline graph); features similar to vascular Parkinson's. (Book p581)

questions.q: A small-vessel patient with gait apraxia, magnetic foot and falls - which tract's lower-limb fibres (close to the ventricle) are affected per the table?
questions.exp: Fibres affected -> manifestation: corticobulbar tract -> pseudobulbar palsy; corticospinal tract (affects lower limb fibres close to the ventricle) -> gait disturbances and falls, gait apraxia, magnetic/ignition foot phenomenon (feet 'stuck' to floor); fibres from paracentral lobule -> urinary abnormalities; corticostriate fibres (PFC to striatum) -> personality changes. (Book p581)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item NOT a feature of cerebral amyloid angiopathy:
questions.exp: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy: A-beta 40 protein deposition, elderly, microhemorrhages. (NOTCH3 is the CADASIL mutation.) (Book p581)

questions.q: CADASIL is the m/c inherited vascular dementia with which mutation and presentation?
questions.exp: CADASIL: cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with small vessel ischemic change/leukoencephalopathy, or CADA with stroke and ischemic leukoencephalopathy; m/c inherited vascular dementia; NOTCH3 mutation; presentation aura + migraine + dementia + stroke. (Book p582)

questions.q: The NPH hydrocephalus tree places aqueductal stenosis under which branch?
questions.exp: Hydrocephalus: occlusive (non-communicating) -> aqueductal stenosis; non-occlusive (communicating) -> up CSF production or down CSF adsorption -> idiopathic (NPH) / familial (congenital: arachnoid granulations; acquired: trauma, SAH). Note: atrophy - obtuse interventricular angle. (Book p582)

questions.q: NPH per the page: the GUD abnormalities, CSF profile and Rx are:
opts: Gait apraxia (magnetic foot), urinary incontinence, subcortical dementia; normal CSF pressure (20 ml/day produced); shunting
Spastic paraparesis, urgency, cortical dementia; raised CSF pressure; acetazolamide
Tremor, ataxia, aphasia; low CSF pressure; fenestration
Apraxia, incontinence, amnesia; xanthochromic CSF; shunt revision
questions.exp: NPH pathology: adsorption defect > outflow resistance of CSF -> ventriculomegaly, no atrophy. Clinical: symptoms progress over weeks to months; GUD - gait (gait apraxia/magnetic foot), urinary (incontinence), dementia (subcortical type); arrest in initiation of ambulation; gait instability with multiple falls; generalized slow movements; CSF pressure normal (20 ml/day produced); Rx shunting (good prognosis if effective); MRI - interventricular angle acute. (Book p582)

units.guide:
FTD/Pick's: sporadic proportion, MAPT proteins, behavioural variant and the tauopathy/PFC notes.
DLB opens with its rank and the Parkinson-plus components; the DLB-versus-PD table and rocket sign follow.

units.title: 2. Subcortical vs Cortical & Prion
units.guide:
The subcortical-versus-cortical table is read row by row.
Prion disease opens with its definition, the four types and the CJD block.

Large-vessel criteria and the stroke-dementia relationship open the vascular block.
Small vessel disease (Binswanger, CAA, CADASIL) and the NPH tree/triad close the chapter.
